meanings: заувек, увек, још увек or одувек?

examples.en: I always get up at seven.

examples.sr: Мој деда [о̀дуве̄к] живи у овом селу.
examples.en: My grandfather has lived in this village since forever.

related.en: forever — about the future: something that will never change
always — it repeats every time, at any moment
still — the state continues up to now
since forever, all along — from time immemorial up to today

note: Same root, different meanings: «заувек» looks forward, «одувек» looks back, «увек» is about constancy, «још увек» says that nothing has ended yet.

examples.en: Grandpa sharpens the scythe before the mowing.

related.en: hair — what grows on the head; singular, «моја коса»
scythe — a tool for mowing grass; plural «косе»
slanting, oblique (f. of «кос») — an adjective: a line that is not straight

note: The words are spelled the same and differ only by context (and by stress and length in speech). The sentence always makes the meaning clear.

meanings: to burn or to tan: загорети, препланути or изгорети на сунцу?

examples.sr: Ручак је [заго̀рео] јер сам заборавио шпорет.
examples.en: Lunch got burnt because I forgot about the stove.

examples.sr: После одмора на мору сва је [прѐпланула].
examples.en: After a vacation at the seaside she's all tanned.

examples.sr: Заспао сам на плажи и [изго̀рео] на сунцу.
examples.en: I fell asleep on the beach and got sunburned.

related.en: to burn, to get scorched — about food or something on the fire; of a suntan only rarely, in bookish style («загорело лице»)
to get tanned — to get a nice tan; «поцрнети» also works
to get sunburned — when the skin turns red and hurts

note: «Загорети» is first of all "to burn" (food). For a tan say «препланути» or «поцрнети», for a sunburn «изгорети на сунцу».
A pigeon says «гу-гу-гу», a sparrow «жив-жив», a mouse «цију» or «цију-цију», a hen «ко-ко-да», a duck «ква» or «ква-ква», a frog «кре-кре». A cat in the street is called with «мац-мац».
title: Animal sounds: a slide series

note: Serbian names have short informal versions, and they don't always look like the full name: Александар - Аца, Валентина - Вања, Марко - Маре, Горан - Гоки. When you meet someone, don't be surprised if in conversation they answer to a completely different word.
title: Nadimak: how a name turns into a nickname

note: Licitar (in Serbia more often «лицидерске») cookies are bright red honey gingerbread decorated with icing. The best-known shape is a heart with a small mirror in the middle; a name may be written on it. They are given as gifts and hung as decorations at Christmas, weddings and fairs. The craft is known in Croatia, Slovenia and Serbia (especially in Vojvodina).

note: A series of cards about verbs of getting drunk, with the Serbian reflexive «се». Mild: «учиркати се» - to get slightly tipsy. Just drunk: «налокати се», «налити се» (literally "to pour oneself full"). Stronger: «урољати се» (plastered), «летвосати се» (absolutely wasted). All colloquial.

related.en: to go well, to come easily
we blew it, it all went wrong

note: A «wrong / the Serbian way» series. Instead of the neutral «знам да то радим добро» people say «иде ми то од руке» (I'm good at it). Instead of «било је ужасно» - «обрали смо бостан» (we really blew it). «То је то» is replaced by «чича-миче и готова прича» (and that's that), «он је лењ» by «лезилебовић» (lazybones), «доста је» by «таман» (that's enough, just right), «шта то причаш» by «лупаш» (you're talking nonsense).
title: Lively Serbian expressions instead of plain ones

note: The suits are called: треф (clubs), каро or ромб (diamonds), херц or срце (hearts), пик (spades). Diamonds and hearts each have two names: a foreign one and a Serbian one. The words come in handy when talking about cards and gambling.
title: Card suits in Serbian

note: In Serbian mythology the ала (or аждаја) is a monster said to cause eclipses by swallowing the sun or the moon. The image often merges with the dragon slain by Saint George on icons. The word «ала» is also familiar as an exclamation like "wow!": that is a different word, but it sounds the same.
title: Ala: a monster from folk belief

note: Many Serbian words came from Greek, sometimes through Turkish or Italian. «Лампа» comes from the Greek «лампа» (a light), «фењер» from the Greek «фанари» (a lantern). The sound changed: Greek «фан-» became Serbian «фењ-».

note: Serbia has three short emergency numbers: 192 - police, 193 - firefighters and rescuers, 194 - ambulance. It's useful to know them as words: that's how signs in shops and offices are labeled.
title: Emergency numbers in Serbia

note: Serbs name the half hour like this: «пола осам» is 7:30, literally "half to eight". It's easy to get wrong and think of 8:30 (compare British "half eight", which does mean 8:30). Other formats: «седам сати и пет минута» is 7:05, «пет минута до седам» is 6:55. The morning starts after midnight: 1 a.m. is «један сат ујутру».
title: «Пола осам» means half past seven

note: Films in Serbia often run under their own titles: «Сам у кући» - Home Alone, «У ствари, љубав» - Love Actually, «Карневалска ноћ» - the Soviet film Carnival Night, «Како је Гринч украо Божић» - How the Grinch Stole Christmas. Useful for searching listings and subtitles.
title: New Year's films in Serbian

note:
Offices often ask for an e-mail address, so you need to name the characters.

• @ — «мајмунче» (little monkey)
• . — «тачка» (dot)
• - — «цртица» (hyphen)
• _ — «доња црта» (underscore)

Example: ana.petrovic@pošta.rs is read «ана тачка петровић мајмунче пошта тачка рс».
title: How to dictate an e-mail address in Serbian

note: Choosing «у» (in, into) or «на» (on, onto) isn't always what an English speaker would expect, so learn these combinations whole. With «на»: на факултет (to the university), на интернет (on the internet), на путовање (on a trip). With «у»: у кујну (to the kitchen), у пошту (to the post office), у куповину (shopping), у шетњу (for a walk), у природу (out into nature), у пензију (into retirement), у иностранство (abroad).
title: «У» and «на»: fixed combinations to learn whole

note: In Serbian a syllable can be built around «р», and then the stress falls on that consonant. It happens in the words «хркати» (to snore), «срце», «прст», «врт», «крв». It's unusual for an English speaker: there is no vowel in the syllable, but the «р» is held like a vowel.
title: Stress on the syllabic «р»
